System Map

The theme is not a list of separate trends. Four loops connect its parts. Schools test in person (B1): more use of AI weakens coursework as proof, which pushes schools towards observed assessment. Fewer first rungs (R1): AI takes routine graduate tasks, entry roles and early experience shrink, and employers lean further on AI. Proven skills earn trust (R2): observed assessment lets a degree vouch for skills, which helps graduates into jobs and brings applicants. The hiring arms race (R3): applicants use AI, employers add their own tests and rules, and the degree counts for less.

Learning and assessment		More use of AI makes take-home coursework weaker proof of learning, weaker coursework pushes schools towards observed assessment, and observed assessment limits what AI can do for a student in graded work.Priming: oral exams return in Spain

Hover over a status for its meaning: Priming means the parts are in place but the circle has not yet closed at scale; Turning means every step in the loop has current evidence, so it is running now.

The Scenario Matrix’s horizontal axis asks whether fewer first rungs (R1) outrun employers reshaping entry roles, that is whether employers or schools train new graduates; its vertical axis asks whether proven skills earn trust (R2) faster than the hiring arms race (R3) erodes it, that is whether the degree or employers’ own tests vouch for skills.

What it means: the loops a school can push hardest are schools testing in person (B1) and proven skills earning trust (R2), and both turn on the same thing: assessment that shows what a student can do without AI doing it for them. The pressure on first jobs comes from outside switches, cheaper AI tools and the economic cycle, which the school does not control. The levers it does control are how it assesses, what it teaches and what it publishes.
